$scopeNote: Only ORDINARY (consumer/creditor judgment) wage garnishment is state-overridable here. Federal law — support orders, federal tax levies, federal student loan default — preempts a state's own wage-exemption statute entirely, so nothing in this file ever changes those two calculations in src/garnishment.ts; only 'consumer_creditor' orders consult it. A state absent from this file entirely has no known departure from the plain federal CCPA default and is computed with it as-is — a narrower claim than 'every state's garnishment law has been fully researched.' A state PRESENT in this file with only a `knownGap` note (no `ordinaryGarnishmentProhibited`/`ordinaryGarnishment`/`headOfFamilyOrdinaryGarnishment`/`fullExemption` block) means a real departure IS known to exist but isn't modelled yet — also computed against the federal default in the meantime, but disclosed rather than silent. 22 states now carry a modelled override (NJ wired 2026-09-05 via GarnishmentFormula's new povertyGuidelineTier shape; MD wired the same day, on re-research finding its county variation was itself repealed by a 2020 amendment — see MD's own $note); the remaining 28 + DC are the unconfirmed-federal-default baseline described above. No state currently carries only a bare `knownGap` disclosure.

NJ.$note: WIRED 2026-09-05, closing the household-size gap this entry previously disclosed: GarnishmentFormula gained a new povertyGuidelineTier shape (src/registry.ts, src/garnishment.ts) and GarnishmentOrder gained householdSize, the same discipline as ND's dependents or FL's headOfFamily — a caller-asserted fact this engine never guesses. Two modelling choices, both disclosed rather than silent: (1) basis is GROSS, not the CCPA's 'disposable earnings' term of art — the statute's own words ('wages, debts, earnings, salary, income from trust funds or profits due and owing') read as gross, unlike the federal 25% rule which explicitly says disposable; (2) above the 250%-of-poverty threshold, this engine falls through to the plain federal default rather than inventing a fixed NJ number, because the statute itself gives the court discretion there ('may order a larger percentage') rather than naming one — the 25% figure that secondary sources often quote alongside this rule is specifically for debts owed TO THE STATE (a different creditor this engine's GarnishmentOrderType doesn't model at all, not the ordinary consumer_creditor case). The poverty-guideline base/increment are HHS's 2026 48-states-and-DC table and must be re-verified every January when HHS republishes it — see this override's own sources. Absent GarnishmentOrder.householdSize, this falls through to the federal default with an explanatory line rather than assuming a household size, same as an unset headOfFamily. The $48/week flat exemption (2A:17-50) is a separate, additional floor layered on top of the percentage test, not a replacement for it.

MD.$note: WIRED 2026-09-05, closing this entry's own previously-disclosed county-geography gap -- but not the way that gap assumed it would close. Re-researching Maryland's statute for this pass surfaced that the county variation this file's own PRIOR note described is itself STALE: a 2020 amendment to Md. Code, Com. Law 15-601.1 repealed the old Caroline/Kent/Queen Anne's/Worcester carve-out and made the exemption uniform statewide, so there is no more sub-state geography to thread into GarnishmentInput after all -- the correct fix was updating the RESEARCH, not building county plumbing. The resulting statewide rule turns out to be EXACTLY this project's existing Shape A (capFractions + a minimum-wage floor, the same mechanism IL/NY/MA/CT/DE/CO/WA already use) with one substitution: Maryland's own $15.00/hr state minimum wage stands in for the federal $7.25 in the 30x floor test, since 15-601.1 says '30 times the State minimum hourly wage,' not the federal one -- the 25% fraction itself is identical to the federal CCPA default. No new GarnishmentFormula shape or code was needed. Re-verify stateMinimumHourlyWage if Maryland's minimum wage changes.
